articles.title: Taking a deep dive in Helsinki’s subterranean city
articles.summary: Under the Finnish capital lies a world of swimming pools, go-karting tracks, playgrounds – and even an art gallery. The moon is an impostor. Swimming backstroke beneath its surface, I look up at craggy hollows in close relief.
body: This is no lunar landscape but Helsinki’s underground swimming hall, excavated from granite bedrock and officially opened in 1993. These days, Itäkeskus uimahalli is one of the Finnish capital’s most visited leisure facilities, welcoming 400,000 people a year. Local people mingle with tourists, I will discover, during a week exploring Helsinki’s subterranean metropolis.

My visit was one of 12 research trips I made over three years to better understand how cities are being reimagined. It turned into a book, How to Build a City, for which I travelled to locations that are testing the frontiers of urban living in response to an increasingly uncertain world.

Many global cities feature a version below ground, but Helsinki’s is thought to be the only one transformed for peace. As urbanisation increased the population, a more efficient solution was needed for heating plants and telecoms cables. You could scatter them around in expensive pockets of land, digging up the streets and sacrificing parks. Or you could tuck them away beneath ground level, by adding to bomb shelters first carved out during the second world war.

articles.title: You be the judge: should my partner dial down the heat when he cooks?
articles.summary: Rhonda believes Ned ruins woks. He reckons he has famous chefs on his side. You decide whose argument is in flames. • Find out how to get a disagreement settled or become a juror. He whacks the heat right up, which stains our wok and makes it really hard to wash up.
body: My partner, Ned, does most of the cooking in our house and he’s really good at it. I help prep and I usually do the washing up, which is how this issue arose. We had an old wok that became so encrusted with burnt stir-fry it was difficult to clean. Eventually, I said we needed to buy a new wok. We bought an expensive stainless steel one, but we’ve only had it three weeks and it’s stained already.

Ned cooks with the heat turned up as high as possible. I know with a wok you turn the heat up high initially before you put in the meat or vegetables, but you’re supposed to turn it down before you add the sauces. Otherwise, they burn on to the wok and make it difficult to clean. Once you get stainless steel to a certain temperature, it maintains that heat, so you don’t need to keep the flame on maximum. The point of stainless steel is that it stays stainless. If you stain it, you’re overheating it.

Once, when Ned was cooking, I turned the heat down myself. He objected and there was a bit of argy-bargy in the kitchen. I was annoyed because I knew I would be the one scrubbing the wok later, and I had a sore shoulder.

articles.title: Rachel Roddy’s recipe for tomatoes stuffed with breadcrumbs, chickpeas and herbs | A kitchen in Rome
articles.summary: A well-seasoned and comforting meal to ease you into the autumn months. At this time of year, baked tomatoes stuffed with rice and surrounded by a packing-chip sea of potatoes are typical all over central and southern Italy, and in many other places besides.
body: I haven’t included sausagemeat in my version, but if you wish to, squeeze the meat from a couple of pork sausages and crumble it in at the same time as the chickpeas. Seasoning is fundamental here – salt, obviously (a small amount at various stages is better than all at once), as well as a little minced garlic and herbs. While my instinct here is for parsley and either rosemary or sage, dried mint also works wonderfully, as does cinnamon, whose warm, woody sweetness works beautifully with tomatoes, as it does in tomato sauce, but that’s another column.

How long the tomatoes take to bake will depend very much on their ripeness; harder ones need 10-20 minutes more than those with softer shells, but keep an eye on them and leave them to rest for a while before serving. I also think tomatoes stuffed this way benefit from being baked close together in a ceramic oven dish, which is why I baked cubed potatoes separately; some salted yoghurt or mashed courgettes or aubergine are also good accompaniments. As in the best and busiest tavole calde, serve the wrinkled tomatoes just hotter than room temperature.

articles.title: ‘I miss old Google’: readers tell us how they search the internet in the age of AI
articles.summary: A feature called AI Overviews has been a profound change, and the browsing habits of billions of people are shifting. Google has put artificial intelligence at the front and center of its search bar.
body: “AI is driving the most significant upgrade of the Google Search experience ever,” wrote Liz Reid, Google’s vice-president of search, last August. In May, the company said more AI is coming.

As people grow accustomed to AI chatbots, they’re spending more time with Google’s and therefore more time on Google.com. Academic studies are finding that people navigate less to sites beyond Google if an AI Overview can give them a good enough answer, even if the bot cites the sites that feed it. Clicks, also known as traffic, are often the most significant way a website earns money from advertising. Media outlets and website owners are enduring a sustained traffic decline. Large US media companies are suing Google, alleging that AI summaries have redirected and reduced traffic to their sites, cutting into their revenue.

Google said it had not seen a decline in aggregate traffic and that such accusations are based on “flawed methodologies”. Reid, the company’s vice-president of search, wrote last year: “Total organic click volume from Google Search to websites has been relatively stable year-over-year.”

articles.title: From Pet Care to Laundry: Why Everything’s Getting a Fashion Facelift
articles.summary: From Stanley tumblers to luxury laundry, entrepreneurs are turning functional products into cultural brands — using collaborations, fashion-forward design and limited-edition drops to make the everyday desirable.
body: Whether it’s water bottles, pet care, alternative milk or laundry, some of the least glamorous corners of consumer goods are acquiring the kind of cultural cachet once reserved for fashion.

“When was it normal for a laundry brand to partner with Nobu? Never,” says Seyi Oduwole, foresight analyst at The Future Laboratory, referring to stylist-turned-entrepreneur Melissa Holdbrook-Akposoe’s laundry brand, Le Luxe. “But now, with Melissa’s brand identity tied to luxury selfcare, wellbeing and the elevation of the everyday, that’s normal.”

“Consumers still want quality and performance, but they also want products that reflect who they are. Utility and self-expression are no longer separate ideas. People expect both,” says Kate Ridley, chief brand officer at Stanley 1913. “A water bottle, a coffee cup, or a tote can be as intentional a choice as a pair of shoes or a favorite handbag.”

As fashion becomes crowded, and as consumers look beyond clothes for more accessible ways to express taste, the opportunity is moving into less expected corners of the consumer market. The next status symbol might not be hanging in your wardrobe, but sitting in your fridge, your cupboard, or your gym bag.

articles.title: “Aristocrats on Mars”—Simone Rizzo and Loris Messina Share Their Vision for the “Moschino of the Future”
articles.summary: Simone Rizzo and Loris Messina follow in the footsteps of Rossella Jardini, Jeremy Scott, and Adrian Appiolaza and Franco Moschino himself at Moschino.
body: It’s a deceptively simple distinction. For a house whose visual vocabulary has become so recognizable that its own jokes can easily become clichés, the temptation is to turn the archive into a dressing-up box: pick a slogan, throw in a windmill, and call it Moschino. Rizzo and Messina are taking the opposite route. They have looked at the clothes, studied their construction, and, as they put it, “metabolized” what they found. The objective is not reproduction. “We don’t want to reproduce anything he did literally. The only thing we are carrying forward is his spirit and his way of thinking.”

That may be the most revealing thing they’re saying about their new appointment. Because if Franco’s humor has been endlessly imitated, his method has been considerably less so. Rizzo and Messina are interested in the machinery beneath the joke. “For us it is fundamental that irony is in the concept,” they explained. “If irony is in the product, it becomes ornament.”

articles.title: How Empress Of Turned a Devastating Loss Into One of the Year’s Most Dazzling Records
articles.summary: After losing her family home in the LA fires, the musician began the process of rebuilding—and channeled that emotional journey into her fifth album, “Dream House.”
body: The cover of Empress Of ’s fifth album, Dream House, is a cinematic, sun-drenched image of the musician stepping through the doorway of a suburban home, caught between shadow and light as an intense, blinding sunburst flares directly above the entrance. There’s an air of mystery to it, but also a sense of hopefulness: She’s a woman on the threshold (quite literally) of a new beginning.

But it’s a new beginning with a heartbreaking backstory. In January 2025, the artist behind the project, Lorely Rodriguez, saw her childhood home in Altadena completely destroyed by the Eaton Fire. In the aftermath of the blaze, she and her mom set about rebuilding—and slowly, after many months of grieving the possessions and previous self that had been lost, Rodriguez began writing music again.

articles.title: All That’s Fit to Print: Legendary Stylist Marie-Amélie Sauvé’s New Book Is a Chic Lesson in Fashion History
articles.summary: Marie-Amélie Sauvé’s new book will teach you all the best fashion history.
body: Among the striking, seductive and undeniably stylish photos that make up The World To Come: Visions of an Image Maker, a book that opens a window into stylist and creative director Marie-Amélie Sauve’ s extensive body of work, there is one that stands out for a different reason. It captures a moment of sheer giddiness between Sauvé and Nicolas Ghesquière from his Balenciaga days when she was his fit model. Whatever prompted this outburst of giggling, the photo attests to the closeness they established early on as their respective careers were rising.

Arriving on October 8th, the tome in all its chicness starts off with Polaroid and hazy film throwbacks to this era 30 years ago chez Balenciaga and beyond, when today’s established fashion figures such as Inez van Lamsweerde and Vinoodh Matadin or PR Consulting’s Pierre Rougier brought a fresh and, sometimes disruptive way of doing things to the industry. Interspersed with cerebral essays by the likes of Donatien Grau, Alexander Fury, Emanuele Coccia and Sophie Abriat, the sections gain slickness as Sauvé shifts into stylist mode, shaping editorials and campaigns for major magazines and luxury houses.
points: Marie-Amélie Sauvé’s new book will teach you all the best fashion history.

This year, we decided to throw a one-of-a-kind party at the legendary Tam O’Shanter, an Old Hollywood haunt in Atwater Village with an interior aesthetic that falls squarely between a 19th-century Scottish tavern and Snow White’s house (it was Walt Disney’s favorite restaurant, after all). Inside, we gathered a (frankly insane) lineup of Eater faves, including Holbox, Thunderbolt / Night on Earth, Pasjoli, Café Telegrama, Lawry’s, Quarter Sheets, Ji Rong, Kidori, Molly Baz for Mister’s ice cream sandwiches, and even flown-in out-of-towners including New York City hotspot Dean’s and Gregory Gourdet of Portland’s Kann. Frankly, there’s never really been a food party quite like this.
